li.a: Sydney Morning Herald: Hungry like the wolf
Taiwan News: Declassified secret documents show close ties between Taiwan KMT, Bamboo Union before 1984
Los Angeles Times: Taiwan Frees Newsman's Killers
Taipei Times: US court sentences Bamboo Union gang hitman to life in jail
Taipei Times: The rise and fall of crime boss Chen Chi-li
Foreign Policy: The List, The World's Most Dangerous Gangs

content.p: The Bamboo Union began as a street gang of schoolboys in the suburbs of Taipei and grew into what the Sydney Morning Herald calls one of Taiwan's most powerful triad organisations. It is also known as the United Bamboo Gang. Its name is tied to two things in particular: an arrangement with the ruling Kuomintang (KMT) that, according to testimony from Chen Chi-li, let it commit racketeering in return for political muscle, and the 1984 murder of the writer Henry Liu in California, which, the Herald wrote, became headline news in the United States.

Much of what is known about the gang comes from journalism, court reports and declassified government files, and some of it from the recollections of former members. Where those accounts differ, they are set out below with the name of whoever made each claim.

The Taipei Times reported that the gang was created in Yonghe, then in Taipei County, by the disaffected children of mainlander parents. They banded together to defend themselves against beatings by Hokklo gang members. Because so many of them came from military families, the paper said, the group was better organised than its rivals and readier to use violence. It soon became a force in Taipei.

The Sydney Morning Herald, in a 2014 profile of Chang An-lo, gave a closer view of those years. Chang's parents had brought him from Nanjing to Taipei, where he was two years old in 1950. They were low-ranking exiles who struggled to make a living, and by primary school he was fighting alongside a gang of former mainland boys against crews of local Taiwanese. At 16, according to the same account, he became a full member, and the initiation was to drink a glass of wine with drops of the other members' blood in it. He took the name Bai Lang, or White Wolf, from a bandit leader who raided towns in central China in the early 1900s. His schoolmate and "elder brother" Chen Chi-li was nicknamed "Dry Duck" because he could not swim.

The money came from protection. The Herald wrote that the gang extorted shops and factories, and that its income swelled in the late 1960s, when American soldiers on leave from the Vietnam War crowded into Taipei. Nightclub owners, mostly recent arrivals from the mainland, welcomed Bamboo Union members into their premises to push out rival ethnic Taiwanese gangs chasing a share of gambling, prostitution and drugs. By then, the paper said, the gang was turning into a transnational syndicate.

The Taipei Times tied the gang's growth to Taiwan's politics. The pro-democracy movement was gaining ground by the late 1970s, following two flashpoints, the Chungli Incident in 1977 and the Kaohsiung Incident in 1979. The KMT government realised that its heavy-handed methods were hurting its image. According to the paper, it gave the Bamboo Union a degree of immunity in return for a commitment to use force against the democracy movement. After the Kaohsiung Incident, senior KMT officials met Chen Chi-li, by then the gang's leader, and asked him to use his influence to "serve the country".

The Sydney Morning Herald put the deal at 1979, citing testimony from Chen: the KMT, it said, outsourced political violence to the gang and ignored its racketeering. By the early 1980s the Herald described an organisation with thousands of members in Chinese-speaking communities, the United States and Europe, and later put its size at around 40,000 before the crackdown that followed Liu's death. That figure is the Herald's alone. The Foreign Policy list of dangerous gangs, published in 2008, gave a far smaller membership, about 10,000, mostly ethnic Chinese members and associates living in Taiwan.

Files released under the government's transitional justice effort, analysed by the magazine Mirror Media and reported by Taiwan News in 2020, point the same way. They suggested that before the mid-1980s some gangsters were employed by government and news agencies, among them the National Security Bureau and the Intelligence Bureau, and that some worked as close aides to Chiang Hsiao-yung, a grandson of Chiang Kai-shek. Since 1960, the documents indicated, up to 19 Bamboo Union members had reached top government positions after graduating from military, police and intelligence academies. They also showed the gang reaching abroad in the 1970s, with operations in the United States, Hong Kong, Japan and the Philippines. One declassified document said that in the early 1980s a Philippine provincial governor, who is not named, sold large quantities of arms to a convicted murderer and drug dealer, Liu Huan-rong, who was executed in Taiwan in 1993.

Henry Liu, who wrote as Jiang Nan, was a Chinese-American writer. The Los Angeles Times described him as a writer for the Chinese-language San Francisco Journal who had written a critical biography of President Chiang Ching-kuo. He was 52 when he was shot in the garage of his home in Daly City, a suburb of San Francisco.

The Sydney Morning Herald gave the date as 15 October 1984. The Taipei Times reported that Chen and a few fellow members travelled to San Francisco that October and killed Liu before the biography was complete. Chen was arrested in Taiwan about a month later, during a crackdown on criminal gangs.

At his trial, the Taipei Times said, Chen testified that he acted on the request of Admiral Wang Hsi-ling, who ran the Military Intelligence Bureau and who suspected Liu of working as a spy for Taiwan, China and the United States. Wang later admitted in court that he had given Chen the order, out of patriotism, the paper reported. Chen and Wang were sentenced to prison. The Los Angeles Times reported that Chen and Wu Dun were convicted in 1986 of the murder, which it said was carried out on the order of Wang. The Sydney Morning Herald wrote that Chen and two other members were sentenced to life.

Who stood behind Wang is still disputed. Taiwan News noted that the "ultimate hand" behind the killing remains hidden under competing accounts. Liu Mao-chuan, described as a close partner of Chen, told Mirror Media that Chiang Hsiao-wu, another grandson of Chiang Kai-shek, sent the two gangsters through Wang. The Herald reported that Chang An-lo supplied a tape recording showing the killers had been trained and briefed by Taiwanese military intelligence, and that he implicated the president's son. Taiwan News said that Chang broke the news in the United States that the KMT was responsible, and that this soured the relationship between the party and the gang.

The Herald said Chang was already in a federal penitentiary in Kansas at the time of the fallout. He had been picked up first on a visa violation and then jailed over links to a large US heroin case, which it described as a plan to import 300 kilograms. In 1986 he was sentenced to 15 years for conspiracy to distribute narcotics. By the time he came out in the early 1990s, the paper said, he had collected five bachelor's degrees.

Chen and Wu were freed on parole from Kweishan Prison near Taipei in January 1991, aged 47 and 40, the Los Angeles Times reported. The Taipei Times said Chen served six years. In 1996 he learned he was again wanted by the authorities and went to Cambodia. A senior Taipei prosecutor told the paper, without being named, that after his release Chen had rejoined the gang and kept up criminal activity. In 2000 he gave an interview to Taiwanese media at his Phnom Penh home in which he displayed weapons on camera; Cambodian police arrested him that July on charges of illegal weapons possession and involvement in organised crime. He was released in August 2001 after 13 months. He died in 2007, and the Taipei Times reported that after his death fellow gangsters, some celebrities and media began portraying him as a patriot and hero, and that President Chen Shui-bian complained that the media should not turn a gangster into a hero.

Chang left Taiwan again in 1996, the Herald said, after a new arrest warrant was issued during a fresh crackdown on triads. He took refuge in southern mainland China, and returned in 2013 to lead a pro-unification group, the China Unification Promotion Party. The Herald said he was on Taiwan's most-wanted list for 17 years and was often called the Bamboo Union's "spiritual godfather". In the Herald's interview he said that the people who followed him to the Legislative Yuan in 2014 were "not Bamboo Union people". The paper also reported that police had raided a branch of his party the year before, alleging that it was a front for a Bamboo Union protege engaged in extortion, illegal firearms, drugs and rape. Chang's eldest son, the Herald said, died in 1998 in a stabbing outside a Taipei karaoke club, the work of members of a rival gang, the paper said.

The Bamboo Union's activities outside Taiwan have drawn court cases of their own. In March 2013 a judge in Las Vegas, Michael Villani, sentenced Bai Xiao Ye, 26, to life without parole, with 32 to 85 further years added. The Taipei Times said he was convicted of murder, kidnapping, extortion and conspiracy to commit murder. Prosecutors alleged he worked for the Taiwan-based gang, which they said operated in California and Nevada casinos, and had been sent to collect a US$10,000 gambling debt from Li Wen Jun. Li was stabbed 32 times at a karaoke bar near the Las Vegas Strip in July 2009, and two other people who tried to help him were also hurt. Bai's former girlfriend was given two years of probation as an accessory and testified against him. Bai also faced a California charge over a shooting outside a Los Angeles karaoke bar. The sources do not say how that case ended.

Foreign Policy's 2008 list claimed the group was involved in drug smuggling, human trafficking and gunrunning, with links to the Chinese triads and the Japanese yakuza. It said Taiwan's National Security Bureau believed the gang's drug trade had reached North Korea, a claim the magazine attributed to the bureau. It noted that a 10-kilometre procession of men in black shirts followed the 2005 funeral of Hsu Hai-ching, a one-time leader who died at 93, as a sign the gang remained a force.
